title: Paraeus and Ames: generic vs specific object — quae justificat and qua justificat
source_text: XXV. Eadem est doctrina Paraei in Bellarmini librum primum de Justificatione, cap. 8. ubi affirmat objectum fidei genericum esse omnia quae Deus in verbo suo revelavit; specificum, promissionem specialis misericordiae. Affini quoque ratione Amesius distinguit inter objectum fidei quae justificat, & qua justificat. Et facile concedit fidei quae justificat objectum tam late patere quam Dei verbum; sed fidei qua justificat objectum restringit ad promissionem misericordiae: Et misericordiam illam concedit esse specialem, sed observat nos per misericordiam specialem non intelligere eam quae fidem antecedat, sed quae per ipsam fidem specialis evadit. Quibus verbis significat fidem hominem non justificare, quia credit sibi esse remissa peccata, sed quia per fidem ad Christum confugit, ut sibi in particulari peccata remittantur, & confidit sibi esse remittenda; qua fide remissionem peccatorum reipsa obtinet. Et propterea quoque in sequentibus dicit proprium objectum fidei justificantis, qua talis, non esse propositionem aliquam, sed Christum ipsum, in quo acquiescit ad justificationem a Deo consequendam. Nempe, quia vult fidem proprie non justificare, quatenus credit veram propositionem aliquam, quaecunque tamen illa sit; sed quatenus ad Christum confugit & eo innititur, ut per eum misericordiam, & peccatorum veniam consequatur. In Bellarmini Enervato, libr. 6. cap. 1. & 2. num. 22.
pass_a_gloss: The same is the doctrine of Paraeus on Bellarmine's first book on Justification, chapter 8, where he affirms that the generic object of faith is all things which God has revealed in His word; the specific, the promise of special mercy. By a kindred reason also Ames distinguishes between the object of the faith which justifies, and that by which it justifies. And he readily concedes that for the faith which justifies the object stretches as widely as God's word; but for the faith by which it justifies he restricts the object to the promise of mercy: And he concedes that that mercy is special, but observes that by special mercy we do not understand that which precedes faith, but that which through faith itself becomes special. By which words he signifies that faith does not justify a man because he believes sins to have been remitted to him, but because through faith he flees to Christ, that sins may be remitted to him in particular, and trusts that they are to be remitted to him; by which faith he in very deed obtains remission of sins. And therefore also in what follows he says the proper object of justifying faith, as such, is not some proposition, but Christ Himself, in whom he rests unto obtaining justification from God. Namely, because he will have faith properly not justify insofar as it believes some true proposition, whichever it may be; but insofar as it flees to Christ and leans on Him, that through Him it may obtain mercy and pardon of sins. In Bellarmine Enervated, book 6, chapters 1 and 2, number 22.
pass_b_english: Paraeus: generic object = all God revealed; specific = promise of special mercy.
Ames: object of faith which justifies vs by which it justifies.
Which-justifies spans the whole Word; by-which restricts to the promise of mercy.
Special mercy follows faith — it does not precede it.
Faith justifies by fleeing to Christ for particular remission, not by believing sins already remitted.
Proper object as such: Christ Himself, not a bare proposition.
